docs.title: QGIS Plugin/Interface Widgets and Text Are Distorted and Scaled Incorrectly
docs.text:
This is a problem linked to display settings caused by the connection of multiple monitors and/or varying display scales and resolutions, rather than a QGIS or plugin-related issue. This is backed by a Microsoft support post, linked here, highlighting the issues that may be experienced when using a high-DPI device, such as a 4k monitor. Additionally, in the scaling display setting, Microsoft indicates that entering a custom scaling size between 100% - 500% is not recommended as "...it can cause text and apps to become unreadable."

Possible solutions to this are: - Adjust the scale for all monitors to 100%. - Ensure that the display resolution is the same for both monitors. i.e. If the smallest monitor is set to 1920 x 1080 set the 4k monitor to this display resolution as well.

docs.title: Publications
docs.text:
• Leveraging geospatial data to evaluate women's employment opportunities in the renewable energy sector by Carolina Mayen Huerta Ph.D., Clara Ivanescu, Benjamin Herfort Ph.D., Piero Badowski,Dragos Gontariu. The Renewable Energy (RE) sector has grown significantly in response to the global climate crisis, yet women's participation remains disproportionately low, with many confined to lower-paid, non-technical roles. This persistent gender disparity could limit the sector's potential unless diversity is actively promoted. Traditional studies on women's employment in RE often overlook critical spatial factors, such as access to public transportation, safety, and neighborhood walkability, which are vital for understanding women's job access. To address these gaps, a Geospatial Women's Employment Analytical Framework (GeoWEAF) was developed, identifying 15 key spatial factors across three dimensions: Contextual, Accessibility, and Place-Characterization. These dimensions are crucial for evaluating whether an environment supports women's access to employment in the RE sector. The GeoWEAF was piloted in Saint Lucia to assess its practical application and effectiveness. It was designed as a decision-making tool for policymakers, offering data-driven insights that enable evidence-based decisions accounting for geographic disparities. By integrating spatial indicators into the evaluation of women's employment opportunities, the GeoWEAF provides a comprehensive understanding of the spatial dynamics shaping women's employment prospects, thereby facilitating targeted interventions to promote gender equity in the workforce.
  • A Comparative Assessment of Spatial Factors Influencing Women's Access to High-Skilled Employment in Albania, Bulgaria, and Türkiye by Carolina Mayen Huerta, Clara Ivanescu, Dragos Gontariu. Women’s labor force participation remains limited in many parts of Southeast Europe and surrounding regions, including Albania, Bulgaria, and Türkiye. While prior research has examined social and institutional drivers of low female labor force participation, the influence of geographic factors on women’s access to employment has received comparatively less attention. This study addresses that gap by applying the Geospatial Women’s Employment Analytical Framework (GeoWEAF) to assess how place-based factors shape women’s high-skilled employment opportunities in Albania, Bulgaria, and Türkiye. These countries were selected due to their shared challenges in advancing gender equality in employment, as well as their differing institutional contexts, development trajectories, and stages of European Union integration, making them a valuable basis for comparative analysis. This application modifies the original framework by excluding the environmental hazards factor, given its ambiguous and non-directional effects, and by introducing spatially disaggregated representations of attitudes toward women in STEM and digital inclusion, which were originally applied at the national level. It also revises the methodology for assessing active transport to address data limitations and adjusts both the scoring and weighting schemes to better capture the contextual and spatial variation in the selected countries. The analysis reveals that, although urban areas generally exhibit higher levels of enablement, substantial intra-urban variation persists, with some areas within cities displaying levels of enablement comparable to rural regions. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating spatial analysis into gender and labor market research. Mapping underserved areas in services and infrastructure, and those exhibiting heightened vulnerability to risks, can enhance the targeting of interventions to accelerate women’s inclusion in the workforce.

docs.title: Training Walkthrough
docs.text:
This walkthrough is presented by Tim, lead developer of the GeoE3 plugin, built under contract to the World Bank.

GeoE3 is a tool to help identify areas where we can improve employment and economic outcomes, specifically for women, but it can also be used generically to look at the local population of a country and understand which areas need intervention to improve people's economic outcomes.

This section walks you through from absolute beginning, starting from zero through to having a complete project set up and running for your country of choice, illustrated with screenshots captured step by step. Work through it top to bottom the first time; after that, use it as a reference for whichever dimension you're configuring.

docs.title: Course outline
docs.text:
1. Installation: install QGIS, then the GeoE3 plugin.
  2. The Interface: open the plugin, create a project, and get oriented in the model tree (a right-clickable tree of dimensions, factors and indicators).
  3. The Model: what an indicator, factor, dimension and analysis actually are, how weights aggregate one into the next, and the 0–5 Likert scale every score lands on.
  4. Processor Types: the computation techniques an indicator can use to turn raw data into a score, straight from the PDF report's own Methodology section.
  5. Getting Data: every way GeoE3 sources its input data, from fully automatic downloads to manual research.
  6. Configuring Items: the one generic pattern for configuring any item in the tree.
  7. Contextual Dimension: the national and regional factors that set the baseline for enablement.
  8. Accessibility Dimension: service areas for childcare, healthcare, education and other daily needs.
  9. Place Characterization Dimension: safety, walkability and hazard exposure at the place level.
  10. Running the Analysis: Run All vs Run Incomplete, and recovering from a crash partway through a long run.
  11. Viewing Your Results: interpret the final enablement score, drill into any dimension, factor or indicator.
  12. The Analysis Report: read the PDF report the tool generates after every run, section by section.
  13. Sharing Your Results: export the underlying grid and the study area GeoPackage for use beyond QGIS.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to configure all five Accessibility factors with point data for the facilities they measure, choose an appropriate travel mode and distance thresholds, and understand how service-area buffers turn proximity into a 0–5 score.

The Accessibility Dimension evaluates people's daily mobility by examining their access to essential services. Levels of enablement for work access in this dimension are determined by service areas, which represent the geographic zones that facilities like childcare, supermarkets, universities, banks, and clinics can serve based on proximity. The nearer these facilities are to where people live, the more supportive and enabling the environment becomes for their participation in the workforce. For more information on data input used from open sources, see Getting Data.

Every Accessibility factor uses the Distance by Road technique (see Processor Types). Configure each one using the generic pattern: double-click, point it at the relevant point data, and right-click → Run Item Workflow once you're done.

docs.title: General Overview
docs.text:
This tool evaluates how easily people can access essential services and amenities, considering their potential caregiving roles and daily travel needs. It uses geospatial area analysis with OpenStreetMap (OSM) data to measure accessibility for several factors, including:

  • Women’s Travel Patterns: Access to everyday services like pharmacies, markets, supermarkets, childcare centers, schools and parks.
  • Access to Public Transport: Proximity to bus stops, train stations and other transport facilities.
  • Health Facilities: Availability of clinics, hospitals and other healthcare services.
  • Education and Training Facilities: Distance to colleges, universities and other training centers.
  • Financial Facilities: Access to banks and financial support institutions.

Travel mode: The user can select walking or driving as a travel mode, and it is recommended that the same travel mode should be selected for all accessibility factors. The default travel mode is walking due to its inclusive nature.

Measurement: The default measurement for travel is distance in meters, which is most appropriate for walking. These thresholds are based on evidence from the literature at the factor level and are designed to provide consistency across analyses. If driving is selected as a travel mode, time in minutes is a more appropriate measurement.

Thresholds: They can be adjusted depending on the scope of the analysis—whether it is conducted at a broader scale, such as the national level, or focused on a more localized context, such as urban or regional areas.

💡 Tip: If evidence from the local context suggests alternative thresholds and increments are more appropriate, the user can alter these increments. If the selected travel mode is driving, the equivalent measurement increments should be in minutes and informed by the local context (for example, if evidence suggests the maximum time that women spend driving is 30 minutes, the increments could be 6, 12, 18, 24, 30).

Output: The process generates zones around these amenities, showing how far people can travel on foot or by car within increasing distances or times. Each zone is assigned a score from 5 (high accessibility) to 0 (no accessibility), reflecting decreasing accessibility as distance or travel time increases.

docs.title: Women’s Travel Patterns (WTP)
docs.text:
Women's Travel Patterns (WTP) refer to the unique travel behaviors of women, often involving multiple stops for household or caregiving tasks, making proximity to essential services like markets, supermarkets, childcare centers, primary schools, pharmacies and green spaces crucial. This factor is composed of 5 subfactors which provide additional granularity: kindergartens/childcare, primary schools, groceries, pharmacies and green spaces.

Locate Women's Travel Patterns Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the Women's Travel Patterns section to open the pop-up.
  • 📝 In the Input field, you can select layers already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the shapefiles (point features) corresponding to the indicators by clicking the three-dot button. You can also use the Download from OSM function to extract the latest data from OpenStreetMap.
  • 🔧 Travel mode (optional): Change the travel mode from walking to driving and the measurements from meters to minutes and amend the default thresholds if local context suggests more appropriate increments.
  • ⚖️ Assign Weights: Assign appropriate weights to reflect the relative importance of each factor in the analysis. Ensure these values are consistent with your project objectives, accurately represent the significance of each factor and add up to 1 for a balanced evaluation.
  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factors (optional): If a specific factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • 🔄 Readjust Weights: Weight values must add up to 1 or they're shown in red. After excluding any subfactors, press Balance Weights to reset the remaining ones to an equal share rather than typing each value by hand.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

docs.title: Configuring Items
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to configure any item in the GeoE3 tree (indicator, factor, dimension or the top-level analysis) using the one generic pattern that applies at every level, and set up the analysis item's optional population, mask and job-distribution settings.

Every level of the model tree (indicator, factor, dimension, and the analysis itself) is configured the same way. You'll use this pattern dozens of times over the course of a project, so it's worth learning once, generically, before diving into the per-dimension walkthroughs that follow.

docs.title: The generic pattern
docs.text:
• 🖱️🖱️ Double-click the item to open its configuration dialog.
  • 📝 Point it at data (indicators only): pick a layer already loaded in QGIS, browse to a file, or (for OpenStreetMap-backed indicators) click Download from OSM to fetch it directly.
  • ⚖️ Assign Weights (factors, dimensions and the analysis): set how much each child item contributes, reflecting your project's objectives. The weights must add up to one; if they don't, the values turn red and you can't confirm the dialog.
  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Items: if you don't have data for something, untick its Use checkbox rather than leaving it misconfigured.
  • 🔄 Balance Weights: resets every remaining enabled item to an equal share, rather than you typing each value by hand.
  • ✅ Click OK to confirm.
  • 🖱️ Right-click the item and choose Run Item Workflow.
  • ✔️ A green checkmark confirms it completed successfully.

At the indicator level this is often trivial. For factors whose data was already fetched during project setup (Space2Stats downloads, for example), double-clicking the item shows it's already kind of figured out: the tool has already got that data, and it's configured it for you, so you can just say OK. You get a status icon next to it straight away. Work through every indicator the same way, one by one, picking whichever dataset in your project matches what that indicator needs.

docs.title: Excluding an item you don't have data for
docs.text: Not every factor will have data available. Fragility, Conflict and Violence (FCV), for instance, needs a source like ACLED, or some other proxy like a crime database, and you might not have access to either. In that case, open the parent item (the dimension, in this example), untick Use next to the factor you don't have data for, and press Balance Weights. That resets every remaining enabled factor to an equal share. Give them all equal weighting, for example, and Active Transport is then considered just as important as Water and Sanitation. The excluded factor shows a greyed-out icon, marking it as not part of the analysis.

docs.title: Configuring the analysis
docs.text:
The top-level analysis item (the GeoE3 Score) uses exactly the same dialog pattern as a dimension (weights for its three children: Contextual, Accessibility, Place Characterization), plus a handful of extra, optional settings:

Dimension weights, aggregation boundaries, the GeoE3 by Population demographics source, and the GeoE3 by Job Distribution mask options, all in one dialog.

Aggregation boundaries: set this to, for example, Admin 1, and that means you can then break the results down further by subnational units.

Demographics layer: click Download from S2S and it will fetch population data for you, or provide your own (one common source is WorldPop, which has free, open population data if you need a specific year or a breakdown by age and sex). Supplying this combines female population density with the GeoE3 score to produce the GeoE3 by Population output, a comprehensive dataset of 15 classes: 5 enablement levels × 3 population-density tiers (low/medium/high).

Mask: if you're trying to pilot economic upliftment in specific areas, use a mask layer to filter out cells outside that area. The Global Human Settlements layer masks everything to just where it's highly settled, but you can also use your own raster, buffered points, or a polygon layer.

Job distribution (optional): upload job location data as points, polygons or a raster, with a buffer distance for point data, to see how GeoE3 scores relate to existing or planned job opportunities and restrict the analysis to areas of interest.

Once every dimension is configured, head to Running the Analysis to kick the whole thing off.

Recap

  • One pattern, every level: double-click to configure, assign weights, exclude what you don't have data for, balance weights, OK, then right-click → Run Item Workflow.
  • The analysis item adds optional aggregation boundaries, a population/demographics layer, a mask, and job-distribution data on top of the usual dimension weights.

docs.title: Contextual
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to configure all four Contextual-dimension factors, understand why they're entered as a single national number rather than a spatial dataset, and know which published index backs each one.

The Contextual Dimension refers to the laws and policies that shape workplace gender discrimination, financial autonomy, and overall gender empowerment. Although this dimension may vary between countries due to differences in legal frameworks, it remains consistent within a single country, as national policies and regulations are typically applied uniformly across countries. For more information on data input used from open sources, see the Getting Data tutorial.

Every Contextual factor uses the National Index Score technique (see Processor Types): a researched national score typed straight into the factor's dialog, no spatial dataset involved. Configure each one using the pattern from Configuring Items: double-click, enter the score, then right-click → Run Item Workflow. See Getting Data for how that number is calculated and entered.

docs.title: Generic analysis: the EPLEX score
docs.text:
EPLEX is a summary measure of Employment Protection Legislation (EPL) stringency, created by the International Labour Organization (ILO), that measures how strongly a country's laws protect workers against dismissal at the initiative of an employer.

Enter the EPLEX score as a fraction between 0 and 1 (the tool multiplies it by 5 to put it on the usual 0–5 scale); if you already have a value on the 0–5 scale from an older project, you can enter that directly and it's used as-is.

docs.title: Women's Enabling Environments analysis: the WBL database
docs.text:
For a Women's Enabling Environments analysis, GeoE3 uses data from the WBL (Women, Business and the Law) database instead:

Workplace Discrimination involves laws that address gender biases and stereotypes that hinder women's career advancement, especially in male-dominated fields. It's obtained from the Workplace Index score of the WBL.

Regulatory Frameworks pertain to laws and policies that protect women's employment rights, such as childcare support and parental leave, influencing their workforce participation. This indicator is composed by the Pay and Parenthood Index score of the WBL database.

Financial Inclusion involves laws concerning women's access to financial resources like loans and credit, which is crucial for starting businesses and investing in economic opportunities. This indicator is composed by the Entrepreneurship Index score of the WBL 2024.

The WBL index scores are already 0–100, so you enter the published value directly and GeoE3 converts it to the usual 0–5 scale for you:

As a rough feel for the scale: a country with strongly enabling legislation would score in the 90s; something clearly below that reflects whatever gap you've identified in your research.

docs.title: Getting Data
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll know every way GeoE3 gets its input data — what downloads automatically, what you fetch yourself and import, and what you research and type in by hand — so you can source data confidently for any country, not just the Portugal example used throughout this walkthrough.

Every indicator in the GeoE3 model needs a dataset or a number behind it. There are three distinct ways that data gets into your project:

  1. Automatic, in-app downloads — GeoE3 fetches it for you, no browser required.
  2. Manual download and import — you find a dataset on an external website, download it, and load it into QGIS yourself.
  3. Manual research and entry — for national-level indicators (like workplace discrimination law), you research a published score and type a single number into the plugin.

This page works through each one as a short, self-contained tutorial. Skip to whichever source you need.

docs.title: Pre-built geodatabases for SIDS countries
docs.text: If the country you're analysing is one of the Small Island Developing States (SIDS) covered by the World Bank's original GeoWEAF pilot, you may not need to assemble your own data at all: a ready-made geodatabase already exists. The World Bank Gender Spatial data catalogue collects the spatial GDBs for every SIDS pilot country, pre-built for use with this tool.

docs.title: Tutorial: automatic downloads built into GeoE3
docs.text:
There's another way to get data besides going and fetching it yourself: you can also use the built-in downloader tool, which is based on QuickOSM logic. Click the Download from OSM button inside an indicator's dialog, and it will do a query from OpenStreetMap and fetch down the specific data that indicator needs — childcare facilities, for example, if that's the one you're configuring.

The OSM Download button inside an indicator dialog — here, Women's Travel Patterns.

Note

Quite often the servers are busy and it might fail — I suggest you just keep trying every few minutes until it works for you.

One of the nice things about setting up a project is that if you're doing a regional-scale one, you can also prefetch a bunch of data for your analysis. Tick the box in the setup wizard and click Next, and it's going to go and download a bunch of indicators — a bunch of reference datasets, Space2Stats, that we can use for the analysis.

Tick "Fetch S2S data" during project setup and GeoE3 downloads everything it needs for every Space2Stats-backed indicator.

GHSL (Global Human Settlement Layer) settlement/population classification and Ookla open broadband/mobile coverage also get fetched automatically in the background the first time a workflow needs them — there's nothing to click for those.

This whole process is about collecting data, and there are a bunch of different sources you can fetch it from: there's the Space2Stats program, which is World Bank hosted data; there's OpenStreetMap — which basically you wouldn't get straight from OpenStreetMap, you'd get it from a service like the Geofabrik service below, or using the QuickOSM downloader tool, or using the button inside of the indicator, which also basically uses QuickOSM underneath the hood; or you might get it from your national dataset, from whatever your country's official data sources provide.

docs.title: Tutorial: OpenStreetMap extracts from Geofabrik
docs.text:
For a national or local-scale project — where Space2Stats' regional prefetch doesn't apply — to get busy with actually using the plugin, we need to get some data. What I recommend is to head over to Geofabrik to start off. Geofabrik is an amazing website where they provide extracts from OpenStreetMap for free, and you can just go and download any data you want.

Geofabrik's download server — free OSM extracts, updated daily, organised by continent then country.

Go to the Geofabrik homepage, then Data, then Downloads. Click the link at the top and it's split up by regions, so you just start drilling down to your region — continent, then country (and sometimes there are sub-regions too, for larger countries). You can download it in different ways: individual files, or one big file which has got kind of everything in it — grab the latest free .gpkg.zip (GeoPackage) if it's offered. Once it's downloaded, extract it, add it to QGIS, and right-click the folder in the Browser panel → Add as a Favorite, which will make it easy to work with the data in that folder going forward.

The geopackage is more convenient because you get everything in one single file — you don't have a lot of files all over your hard drive to keep track of. But if there's an error in the file, you can go to plan B, which is to download the shapefiles instead — or use GADM (below) for boundaries specifically.

docs.title: Tutorial: official administrative boundaries from GADM
docs.text:
Sometimes the admin boundary you get from OpenStreetMap or HDX still isn't quite what you want — it might include the coastal maritime area rather than the land boundary you need, or the highest level available might not be the one you're after. If you don't have what you want yet, the next option is to use GADM boundaries.

You could search just for "[your country] official boundary" and see if you can find it published by an official source — quite difficult to do, though if you're working in your own country, maybe you're already familiar with where to get the official data. I happen to know about GADM:

GADM — pick your country, download a GeoPackage of its administrative boundaries at every level.

Here you can also download data by country — choose yours, and again, you can get a geopackage, which is always nicer. It contains one layer per administrative level (ADM_0 for the national boundary, ADM_1 for the first subdivision, and so on) — finally, what we need.

Check the license before you redistribute anything

GADM data is free for academic and non-commercial use. Redistribution or commercial use needs permission from GADM first — see their license page before you publish an analysis built on it.

docs.title: Tutorial: Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX)
docs.text:
Another common source of data is the Humanitarian Data Exchange, HDX for short. GeoE3 does not query it automatically — this is a manual browse-and-download source, the same as Geofabrik or GADM. Punch in your country and you'll see a range of interesting-looking datasets: health, population, airports, railways, buildings, education. Some of these will be useful for you — but you want only the geospatial data, so filter on geodata to narrow it down.

Filtering an HDX search down to geospatial datasets only.

For example, health facilities is going to be one of the things you're interested in for the Accessibility dimension — since it's there on HDX, grab it. (The source is still coming from HDX, though it looks like they get it from HOT OSM.) Open the dataset page, scroll to Data and Resources, and download the shapefile or GeoPackage.

Downloading the point-data resource for a dataset.

HDX is a good first stop for health facilities and some administrative boundary sets, but coverage varies a lot by country — if it doesn't have what you need, fall back to the in-app OSM downloader or Geofabrik.

docs.title: Tutorial: population data from WorldPop
docs.text:
If you want to introduce population into your results (see Configuring Items) and you already ticked Fetch S2S data during project setup, you likely already have a Space2Stats population layer and can skip this. If not, getting it is its own little side quest.

There are various places to get population data. You can go to the Humanitarian Data Exchange — ideally looking for the group you're trying to foster enablement for (women's census population, say), though it's not always there as a clean geospatial layer. Failing that, go to WorldPop. WorldPop is an open data initiative for providing population data for around the world.

Under national boundaries you can download the total population for a given year. But if you want more, you can also get the demographic breakdown — go to Age and sex structures and you can get individual countries from there.

WorldPop's per-country age/sex breakdowns — useful if you want to target a specific demographic, not just total population.

The filename encodes exactly what's inside it — country code, gender, age band, year and resolution — so you can tell at a glance which file has, for example, working-age women.

docs.title: Tutorial: manual national index-score entry
docs.text:
This class of indicators — the four Contextual-dimension factors, EPLEX Score, Workplace Discrimination, Regulatory Frameworks and Financial Inclusion — is calculated using a national score. It assigns one number to the whole dataset based on, for example, what the workplace discrimination environment is like. You need to do your research, find out for your country what level of enablement there is in the legislation, and if it's highly enabling, for example, you'd give it a 95 or plus; if it's some order below that, you'd give it a rating as appropriate.

The table below gives a worked Saint Lucia example and the general sources to use for any other country. If you'd rather skip the lookup entirely, Contextual Dimension lists the Workplace Discrimination, Regulatory Frameworks and Financial Inclusion default score for every country in one table.

docs.title: General sources for other countries
docs.text:
While the table above is specific to Saint Lucia, the same kinds of sources exist for most countries:

  1. World Bank — Women, Business and the Law (WBL): indices on workplace discrimination, regulatory frameworks and financial inclusion.
  2. ILO EPLEX: employment protection legislation index.
  3. UNDP: gender equality, economic participation and sustainable development metrics.
  4. National statistics offices: gender-disaggregated data for contextual and accessibility indicators.
  5. OpenStreetMap: locations of facilities for accessibility and active-transport indicators (via the in-app downloader, Geofabrik, or overpass-turbo.eu directly).
  6. Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX): schools, health facilities and other infrastructure.
  7. World Bank environmental hazards catalogue: fire, flood, landslide, cyclone and drought layers.
  8. Mapillary: crowdsourced street-level imagery, useful for street crossings, sidewalks and public lighting where OSM coverage is thin.
  9. VIIRS Nighttime Lights (NTL): a proxy for safety perception where no dedicated safety-perception dataset exists.

docs.title: Data attribution
docs.text:
GeoE3 pulls from whichever external datasets and services your workflow and inputs actually use — typically some combination of OpenStreetMap, OpenRouteService, GHSL (European Commission JRC), Ookla Open Data, Space2Stats, ACLED and VIIRS Nighttime Lights. When you publish or share an analysis, check and include the attribution, citation text and license/terms for whichever of these you actually used — they're not all the same license.

Recap

  • GeoE3 gets data three ways: automatic in-app download (OSM, Space2Stats, GHSL, Ookla), manual download-and-import (Geofabrik, GADM, HDX, WorldPop), and manual research-and-entry (the four Contextual factors).
  • For a regional-scale project, ticking Fetch S2S data during project setup covers most of your data needs in one step.
  • For national or local-scale projects, you'll do more manual sourcing — Geofabrik for OSM extracts, GADM for clean admin boundaries, HDX and WorldPop for everything else.
  • Check data licenses before you redistribute results — GADM in particular restricts commercial/redistribution use without permission.

docs.title: Viewing Your Results
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to interpret the final GeoE3 score, drill into any dimension, factor or indicator's methodology and weightings, and understand the bivariate legend that results from combining enablement with population density.

This page picks up once the GeoE3 Score has been configured and run (see Configuring Items for assigning dimension weights, adding a population layer or mask, and Running the Analysis for actually kicking off the run). The outputs identify regions where conditions are optimal, or at least favorable, for women to access job opportunities in a specific sector, highlighting key infrastructure investments that could boost women's participation in the workforce.

Once every dimension has been processed (see the three previous pages) and the GeoE3 Score has run, a new layer appears at the analysis node. It's on the same Likert scale as everything underneath it: red cells are very low economic enablement, orange is low, yellow is intermediate, green is enabling, and blue is very enabling.

The completed model tree, with the final GeoE3 Score on the same 0–5 scale as everything beneath it.

We're able to go and explore all of the individual results as well — you can click on any layer and you'll see a description of it at the bottom, in the info panel (you can shrink this panel and resize it back again), including the methodology that was used to calculate it. For example, Workplace Discrimination uses a single factor applied equally to all cells throughout the region.

You can go through and explore the different results generated at the dimension level, then the factor level, and down at the indicator level — remembering that the combination of indicators is combined into the factor. If you double-click on a factor, you can see in a table the weightings used to say what the relative importance of each was in the total assessment. This is the same weights dialog covered in Configuring Items.

docs.title: Visualizing the Outputs
docs.text:
After completing the process, the outputs are automatically added to the Layer Panel in QGIS as a group layer. This group layer has the Mutually Exclusive Group feature activated, which ensures that only one layer within the group can be visible at a time. When this feature is enabled, turning on the visibility of one layer automatically turns off the visibility of the others within the same group, making it easier to compare results without overlapping visualizations.

The outputs consist of all GeoE3 score outputs (aggregated at administrative level, by population, or by job distribution). The aggregated-by-population outputs use a bivariate legend: 5 enablement levels × 3 population tiers, 15 exact classes in total:

Score Class Colour 1 Very low enablement, low population 2 Very low enablement, medium population 3 Very low enablement, high population 4 Low enablement, low population 5 Low enablement, medium population 6 Low enablement, high population 7 Moderately enabling, low population 8 Moderately enabling, medium population 9 Moderately enabling, high population 10 Enabling, low population 11 Enabling, medium population 12 Enabling, high population 13 Highly enabling, low population 14 Highly enabling, medium population 15 Highly enabling, high population

The outputs are stored within the project folder created during the setup phase as raster files. These files can be shared and further utilized for various purposes, such as visualization in QGIS or other GIS software, integration into reports, overlaying with other spatial datasets, or performing advanced geospatial analyses, such as identifying priority areas or conducting trend analysis based on the scores.

If the results do not immediately appear in the Layer Panel after processing the GeoE3 Scores, you can resolve this by either adding them manually from the folder path or by right-clicking on the GeoE3 Score and selecting Add to map from the context menu.

When population and a subnational boundary layer are both configured, Add GeoE3 Aggregates to Map breaks the enablement scores down by subnational district using the same 15-class bivariate legend above — each region shaded by its majority class, from dark red (low enablement, low population) through to bright blue (high enablement, high population).

Each subnational region shaded by its majority class — combining 5 enablement levels with 3 population tiers (low/medium/high) gives the 15 categories in the legend.

There's one more advanced option worth knowing about — the subnational score matrix — covered in The Analysis Report along with the rest of what's in the PDF report.

The GeoE3 Score node has the same right-click menu as any other item (see The Interface), plus several score-specific Add to Map variants:

Menu item What it does Add GeoE3 Score to Map The base 5-class enablement score Add GeoE3 by Population to Map The 15-class bivariate enablement × population score Add GeoE3 Aggregates to Map The subnational breakdown by administrative boundary Add Masked Scores to Map The score restricted to whatever mask you configured Add Job Opportunities Mask to Map The job-distribution mask, if configured Add Study Area to Map The study area boundary itself

Every run also produces a full PDF analysis report, and the raw grid results are available for export to CSV or any GIS format. Both are covered next, in The Analysis Report.

Recap

  • The GeoE3 Score combines the three dimensions you've already configured, weighted and run just like any other item in the tree.
  • Adding a population layer (auto-fetched from Space2Stats, or your own, see WorldPop) unlocks the 15-class bivariate legend: 5 enablement levels × 3 population tiers.
  • Adding a subnational boundary layer breaks results down by region; adding a mask (GHSL settlements, or your own) restricts the analysis to areas you actually care about.
  • The Subnational score matrix setting (Settings → Options → GeoE3, off by default) adds a region-by-factor breakdown table to the PDF report.

docs.title: Installing QGIS & GeoE3
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll have a working QGIS install with the GeoE3 plugin enabled, and know where its settings live if you ever need to change the defaults.

GeoE3 runs inside QGIS as a regular plugin, so there's nothing to compile or configure beyond what's covered here.

docs.title: Installing QGIS
docs.text:
• A recent QGIS 3.x install (QGIS 3.28 or later is recommended).
  • Internet access the first time you run an analysis, since several processing steps fetch open data (OpenStreetMap, population rasters, humanitarian data) on demand.
  • Enough disk space for your study area's working files (national-scale analyses can use several gigabytes).

docs.title: Installing the plugin
docs.text: Follow the steps below to install the GEOE3 QGIS plugin.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Plugin Manager in QGIS
docs.text:
1. Launch QGIS.
    1. Go to Plugins > Manage and Install Plugins….

docs.title: Step 2: Install the Plugin
docs.text:
1. In the Plugin Manager window, select the All tab in the Plugin Manager.
    1. Search for GEOE3.
    1. Select the plugin and click Install Plugin.

docs.title: Step 3: Verify the Installation and Configure the Tool
docs.text:
1. After installation, check the QGIS toolbar for the new GEOE3 icon Show/Hide GEOE3 Panel.
    1. If the icon is not visible, go to Plugins > Manage and Install Plugins…, then click on the Installed tab.
    1. In the list, find Geospatial Enabling Environments for Employment Spatial Tool (GEOE3) and ensure the checkbox is ticked. The GEOE3 panel should now appear in the QGIS interface.

Recap

  • GeoE3 is a regular QGIS plugin, installed from the Plugin Manager. Search for GEOE3 under the All tab.
  • A toolbar icon and a dockable panel appear once it's installed and enabled under the Installed tab.
  • The default settings in Settings → Options → GEOE3 Settings are recommended for most users; chunk size and concurrent tasks are the two worth revisiting on a particularly powerful (or weak) machine.

Next: The Interface, opening the plugin, creating your first project, and getting oriented in the model tree.

docs.title: The Interface
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to open GeoE3, create a new analysis project from a boundary layer, choose the right scale for your study area, set up a routing environment, and read the dock's tree view, including the status icons and right-click menu every other page in this walkthrough relies on.

This page assumes you've already installed QGIS and the GeoE3 plugin and have some data to work with. If not, see Getting Data first.

docs.title: Opening the plugin
docs.text:
Once installed, you'll find GeoE3's icon in the QGIS toolbar. Click it to open the panel, which docks to the right-hand side of the window by default.

  1. Locate the Toolbar Icon Find the plugin's icon in the QGIS toolbar.

  2. Open the Plugin Click on the plugin's toolbar icon to open its main window.

The first page is a short welcome and overview; the next explains what the tool does and who built it. Use the arrow buttons at the bottom of the panel to move between pages.

The welcome panel.

docs.title: Opening or creating a project
docs.text:
Next, GeoE3 asks you to choose a project folder — every analysis lives in its own folder, which the plugin manages for you.

Open an Existing Project loads a project folder you've already set up and configured — pick this to carry on where you left off.

Create a New Project walks you through setting one up from scratch, which is what the rest of this page covers.

Warning

The folder you choose must be empty. GeoE3 treats everything in it as its own — using a folder that already has other files in it can lead to errors or accidental overwrites. Give it a descriptive name (country/region plus a date is a good pattern) so you can find it again later.

docs.title: Creating a new project
docs.text:
Choose Create a New Project, then browse to the empty working folder you made earlier and use that as the project folder. Then you've got three choices to pick from to define the scale of your analysis:

Scale Typical use Default grid size Regional Quick analysis, multi-country or continental study ~30 km (hex grid) National A single country 1,000 m (1 km) Local A city or small region 100 m

In all three cases you can change the grid size if you want to, but the defaults are a reasonable place to start. Regional scale also unlocks the Space2Stats prefetch step covered in Getting Data.

Scale, grid size, boundary layer and the Women's Enabling Environments toggle, all in one step.

Then it asks for the boundary layer — point it at your Admin0 (national boundary) layer, and tell it which column has the country name. If your boundary layer doesn't look like the typical boundary you'd expect (it still extends out into the ocean, for example, or is missing the level you need), see the GADM and HDX tutorials — OpenStreetMap's admin boundaries aren't always reliable.

The last thing it asks is whether you want to do a Women's Enabling Environment study, or just a generic economic enabling-environment study. Leave Women's Enabling Environments ticked for the GeoWEAF-framework analysis this walkthrough demonstrates; untick it for the generic one, and you'll get a slightly different workflow — some women-specific factors get disabled, and the Contextual dimension needs an EPLEX score instead of individual factor analysis.

docs.title: What happens next: the study area grid
docs.text:
Once you confirm, it computes a grid across the study area and writes that into a GeoPackage file — you can see it in the study area. It creates various different products: the main thing is the GeoPackage, which contains a regular grid (for a regional analysis this is an H3 grid, so hexagons covering the whole study area; national and local scale use square grid cells instead), and it also contains masks. A mask is a raster layer which covers the study area, excluding any pixels outside the area by giving them NoData, and including any areas inside the study area by giving them a value of one.

When it finishes, a Study Area Report opens automatically, summarizing how many grid cells were created, how long each part of the country took to process, and where the generated files live (your project folder's study_area/ subfolder). You can reopen it any time.

docs.title: Setting up routing
docs.text:
The next thing it wants to do is set up the routing environment. For some analysis steps we use a routing analysis that allows us to understand, for example, what's the travel time for a woman to move from her home to a clinic (or what have you) using the road network. It's possible to use OpenRouteService for this, but you need an API key — or you can use the native QGIS routing (native:serviceareafromlayer), which is a bit slower but doesn't require any keys.

Either way, it wants to know if you've got a road network. If you've already downloaded OSM data (see Getting Data), you probably don't want to use the railways — you want the roads layer. If it's in the wrong coordinate reference system, GeoE3 will reproject it into the correct one for you automatically. If you don't have a road dataset, you can also click the Download from OpenStreetMap button and it will fetch one for you from Geofabrik or OpenStreetMap directly.

docs.title: Reading the dock: a tree of dimensions, factors and indicators
docs.text:
Once you click through, you land on the model tree (the main working view you'll spend most of your time in). It organises the different types of analysis outputs into three categories, which we call dimensions: the Contextual dimension, the Accessibility dimension, and the Place Characterization dimension. Those are further subdivided into factors (the second-level grouping), and each dimension may have one or more factors associated with it.

The complete model tree for a Women's Enabling Environments analysis (3 dimensions, 16 factors, 35 indicators).

It's a tree in the literal QGIS-layer-panel sense: expand a dimension to see its factors, expand a factor to see its indicators. What each of these levels actually means, and how they combine, is the subject of The Model. This page is just about finding your way around the panel itself.

The data processing interface: dimensions and factors on the left, status widgets on the right.

Status widgets. Each row in the tree shows a small icon telling you what state that item is in:

Status Meaning Configured, not run Inputs are set up but the workflow hasn't been executed yet Required, not configured Essential inputs are still missing Completed successfully Processing finished without errors Workflow failed Something went wrong (needs troubleshooting) Not configured (optional) Optional inputs, left unset Excluded from analysis Deliberately disabled, won't be run or counted

docs.title: Right-click to interact with items
docs.text:
Every item in the tree (indicator, factor, dimension or the top-level analysis) responds to the same right-click context menu. This is how you drive the whole tool once an item is configured:

Menu item What it does Run Item Workflow Executes that item's workflow, computing its output Clear Item Removes the item's results so you can reconfigure and rerun it Clear Results Clears all previously generated results Show Attributes Displays detailed attribute data for the item Add to Map Adds the item's output layer group to the QGIS Layer Panel Open Log File Opens the log file to review the workflow's detailed processing or errors Open Working Directory Opens the folder containing that item's output files

The successful completion of a workflow is always shown by a green checkmark status widget. If results don't automatically appear in the Layer Panel after processing, right-click the item and choose Add to Map.

Tip

If an input value needs to change for any reason (an incorrect initial entry, say), right-click the item and choose Clear Item, then right-click it again and, while holding Shift, choose Run Item Workflow. This reassesses the input and outputs the corrected score.

Run All (bottom of the panel) runs every workflow regardless of status; Run Incomplete only runs the ones that haven't completed yet. The Project button takes you back to the setup pages above if you need to change the scale or boundary layer later, and Help opens the plugin's GitHub documentation.

Configuring every item in this tree (pointing each factor at its data, or entering a researched national score) is exactly what The Model, Processor Types and Configuring Items walk through next.

Recap

  • GeoE3 projects live in their own empty folder; pick Create a New Project to start one from a boundary layer.
  • The scale you choose (regional/national/local) sets a default grid size and, for regional, unlocks the Space2Stats prefetch.
  • Routing for accessibility indicators defaults to QGIS's free native engine; OpenRouteService is faster but needs an API key.
  • The dock is a tree (dimension → factor → indicator), and every row has a status icon and the same right-click menu: Run Item Workflow, Clear Item, Add to Map and the rest.

docs.title: Place Characterization
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to configure all seven Place Characterization factors, choose between the alternative data input options several of them offer, and understand how two of them (Education and Digital Inclusion) combine a national index score with spatial masking or coverage layers rather than raw point data.

The Place Characterization Dimension refers to the social, environmental, and infrastructural attributes of geographical locations, such as walkability, safety, and vulnerability to natural hazards. Unlike the Accessibility Dimension, these factors do not involve mobility but focus on the inherent characteristics of a place that influence people's ability to participate in the workforce. For more information on data input used from open sources, see Getting Data.

Place Characterization factors span almost every processor type: distance buffers, feature counts, published index numbers, ready-made rasters and zone lookups all appear here, and several factors support more than one depending on the data you give them. Configure each one using the generic pattern: double-click, provide its data, and right-click → Run Item Workflow once you're done.

docs.title: General Overview
docs.text:
Place Characterization factors refer to the following indicators:

  • Active Transport: identifies areas based on their capacity to support safe and efficient active transport (walking, cycling, and other non-motorized modes) by analyzing and categorizing the road network features downloaded during the project setup phase.
  • Safety Perception: defines areas perceived as safe based on specific data or, alternatively, on how brightly lit they are, assuming that brightly lit areas are safer than those with no lights.
  • Fragility, conflict and violence (FCV): assigns scores by analyzing overlap with ACLED data and buffers representing various types of events.
  • Education: computes a raster that provides a standardized measure of the percentage of people who have attained higher education within the country or region of interest. The spatial representation of education attainment is confined to inhabited areas as classified by GHS-SMOD. The default classes to be excluded from GHS-SMOD are 10 (Water grid cell) and 11 (Very low density rural grid cell).
  • Digital Inclusion: assesses the availability and accessibility of digital infrastructure by computing a national index score. If local statistics are available, this is used in conjunction with Ookla coverage layers, which supports the spatial representation of the data. Each Ookla polygon receives the DI score and it is further mapped to the raster cell. Raster cells that do not intersect Ookla polygons receive a score of 0 (no access).
  • Environmental Hazards: characterizes areas based on their vulnerability to natural disasters.
  • Water sanitation: assesses the availability and accessibility of clean water and sanitation facilities.

For certain factors, multiple data input options are available depending on the data's format and availability.

As with the Accessibility dimension, Active transport, Safety and Water sanitation factors can be processed according to the level of analysis—whether conducted at a broader scale, such as the national level, or tailored to a more localized context, such as urban or regional areas.

docs.title: Active Transport
docs.text:
Active Transport refers to the availability of walkable environments and cycling infrastructure, recognizing that people often rely on non-motorized modes of travel for daily commutes and errands. It is computed using the OpenStreetMap road network, where road types are classified based on their suitability for walking and cycling.

Locate Active Transport Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the Active Transport section to open the pop-up.
  • 📝 In the Input field, you can select layers already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the shapefiles (point features for street crossings, lines for cycle paths and footpaths and polygons for block layout) corresponding to the indicators by clicking the three-dot button.
  • ⚖️ Assign Weights: Assign appropriate weights to reflect the relative importance of each factor in the analysis. Ensure these values are consistent with your project objectives, accurately represent the significance of each factor and add up to 1 for a balanced evaluation.
  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factors (optional): If a specific factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • 🔄 Readjust Weights: Weight values must add up to 1 or they're shown in red. After excluding any subfactors, press Balance Weights to reset the remaining ones to an equal share rather than typing each value by hand.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

Active Transport factor is calculated based on road types from OpenStreetMap as follows: | Subfactor | Score 0 | Score 1 | Score 2 | Score 3 | Score 4 | Score 5 | |----------------------|------------------|-----------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------| | Key = highway | bus_guideway, escape, raceway, construction and proposed roads | motorway, motorway_link, trunk and trunk_lin | primary, primary_link and track | secondary, secondary_link, unclassified, road, bridleway and service | tertiary and tertiary_link | Pedestrian, Footway, Residential, Living_street, steps | | Key = cycleway | None | N/A | N/A | 1 cycle path | lane, shared_lane, share_busway, track, separate, crossing, shoulder and link | N/A |

docs.title: Safety Perception
docs.text:
Safety Perception addresses the perceived security of public spaces, evaluated through the availability of adequate lighting, which affects women's ability to move freely, seek employment, and access essential services.

Locate Safety Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the Safety section to open the pop-up.
  • 📂 Flexible Data Input Options: Multiple data input options are available depending on the data's availability, format, or geographic coverage. Select one of the following options:
  • 1️⃣ Using Perceived Safety data index score as input:

  • 2️⃣ Using Classified Safety data as input; select the layer already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the shapefiles (polygon features) corresponding to the safety data by clicking the three-dot button and the classification field; this layer will be used for processing:

  • 3️⃣ Using Nighttime Lights data as input; VIIRS Nighttime Lights raster may be used as proxy data for presence of area illumination at night time; select the layer already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the (raster data) corresponding to NTL by clicking the three-dot button; this layer will be used for processing:

  • 4️⃣ Using Street lights data as input; select the layer already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the shapefiles (point locations) representing street lights by clicking the three-dot button; this layer will be used for processing:

  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factors (optional): If this factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

Safety is calculated by generating 20-meter buffers around streetlights using the default thresholds:

Factor Score 0 Score 1 Score 2 Score 3 Score 4 Score 5 Safety No overlap 1-19% intersection 20-39% intersection 40-59% intersection 60-79% intersection 80-100% intersection

Note: Use nighttime light data only if streetlight data is unavailable.

docs.title: FCV
docs.text:
Fragility, conflict and violence (FCV) considers the frequency of events related to political unrest, conflict, and violence in a region, which can increase people's vulnerability and limit their access to employment and essential services.

Locate FCV Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the FCV section to open the pop-up.
  • 📂 Flexible Data Input Options: Multiple data input options are available depending on the data's availability, format, or geographic coverage. Select one of the following options:
  • 1️⃣ Using Point features data as input; select point locations representing data related to fragility, conflict and violence events; a buffer is needed to estimate the spatial impact of these events, the default radius is 5000m but if the impact radius of an event is known, it should be used instead:

  • 2️⃣ Using ACLED data as input; select ACLED data in CSV format representing fragility, conflict, and violence events; this indicator is structured by assigning scores to rasters based on their overlap with buffers indicating different types of events. Using point locations of FCV events, generate circular buffers with a default radius of 5 km to estimate the spatial impact of these events. If the impact radius of an event is known, it should be used instead; a pop-up will appear to validate the CSV format.

  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factor (optional): If this factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

FCV is structured by assigning scores to raster cells based on their overlap with buffers representing different types of events. Using point locations of FCV (Fragility, Conflict, and Violence) events, create circular buffers with a radius of 5 km to estimate the spatial impact. If a specific event's impact radius is known, it should be applied instead. Raster cells intersecting with these default buffers are scored as follows:

Factor Score 0 Score 1 Score 2 Score 3 Score 4 Score 5 FCV battles and explosions explosions and remote violence violence against civilians not applicable protests and riots no overlap with any event

docs.title: Education
docs.text:
Education refers to the proportion of women in a region who have attained higher education, particularly in the specific field of analysis, serving as an indicator of societal attitudes towards women working in that sector. The raster file is filtered by GHSL classes to account only for areas where people live.

Locate Education Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the Education section to open the pop-up.
  • 📂 Flexible Data Input Options: Multiple data input options are available depending on the data's availability, format, or geographic coverage. Select one of the following options:
  • 1️⃣ Using Index score at the national or regional level, based on the proportion of women who have attained higher education as input:

  • 2️⃣ Using Classify Polygon Into Classes data as input; select the layer already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the shapefiles (polygon features) corresponding to the education data by clicking the three-dot button then, select the classification field to be used for processing:

  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factor (optional): If this factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

Education reclassifies the input data to a standardized scale from 0 to 5 using a linear scaling process. In this scale, a score of 5 represents areas where all women have a university degree, while a score of 0 represents areas where no women have a university degree.

docs.title: Digital Inclusion
docs.text:
Digital Inclusion assesses the presence of digital infrastructure in a specific location, which is essential for women to pursue job opportunities, access training and education opportunities, and use financial services. This dataset is masked using the Ookla dataset, to account for areas where internet coverage has been mapped and exclude inhabited areas.

Locate Digital Inclusion Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the Digital Inclusion section to open the pop-up.
  • 📂 Flexible Data Input Options: Multiple data input options are available depending on the data's availability, format, or geographic coverage. Select one of the following options:
  • 1️⃣ Using Index score at the national or regional level, based on the proportion of available digital infrastructure as input:

  • 2️⃣ Using Classify Polygon Into Classes data as input; select the layer already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the shapefiles (polygon features) corresponding to the digital inclusion data by clicking the three-dot button then, select the classification field to be used for processing:

  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factor (optional): If this factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

Digital Inclusion reclassifies input data to a standardized scale of 0 to 5 using a linear scaling process, where 5 represents areas where 100% of households have internet access, and 0 represents areas where no households have internet access.

docs.title: Environmental Hazards
docs.text:
Environmental Hazards relate to the impact of environmental risks, such as floods, droughts, landslides, fires and extreme weather events, which can disrupt job stability, particularly for women in vulnerable sectors.

This factor is composed, by default, of five subfactors representing different types of hazards: fires, floods, landslides, tropical cyclones and droughts. These subfactors are aggregated into a single factor, referred to as Environmental Hazards, based on the selected weights assigned to each subfactor.

If data for one or more hazard types is not available, these subfactors can be excluded from the processing. In such cases, the tool will automatically adjust the weights of the remaining subfactors to ensure accurate aggregation.

The thresholds for defining hazard levels are based on a predefined scoring list. The input data relies on globally available open data sources and is reclassified for use within the tool. However, if more precise and localized data is available, users are encouraged to incorporate it into the processing. In doing so, users should align the data with the thresholds provided to maintain consistency and reliability.

Locate Environmental Hazards Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the Environmental Hazards section to open the pop-up.
  • 📝 In the Input field, you can select layers already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the raster features corresponding to the indicators by clicking the three-dot button.
  • ⚖️ Assign Weights: Assign appropriate weights to reflect the relative importance of each factor in the analysis. Ensure these values are consistent with your project objectives, accurately represent the significance of each factor and add up to 1 for a balanced evaluation.
  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factors (optional): If a specific factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • 🔄 Readjust Weights: Weight values must add up to 1 or they're shown in red. After excluding any subfactors, press Balance Weights to reset the remaining ones to an equal share rather than typing each value by hand.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

Environmental Hazards reclassifies input data to a standardized scale of 0 to 5 using a linear scaling process, where 5 represents areas with no environmental hazards and 0 represents areas with the highest level of hazard.
