docs.title: Water sanitation
docs.text:
Water sanitation concerns the availability of clean water and sanitation facilities, affecting women's time allocation and capacity to engage in employment. It is captured indirectly, by accounting for the spatial distribution of facilities whose operation depends on reliable water supply and sanitation services. The presence of these points of interest suggests the existence of minimum water and sanitation infrastructure necessary for service delivery, even where direct household level data are unavailable.

Locate Water sanitation Section

  • 🖱️🖱️ Double-click on the Water sanitation section to open the pop-up.
  • 📝 In the Input field, you can select layers already loaded in the QGIS Layer Panel from the dropdown menu or manually enter the file path for the shapefiles (point features) corresponding to the points of interest by clicking the three-dot button; a buffer is needed to estimate the spatial impact of these facilities, the default radius is set to 1000 meters; however, this value can be adjusted based on the user's considerations.
  • 🚫 Exclude Unused Factor (optional): If this specific factor is not intended to be included in the process, uncheck the Use button associated with it.
  • ✅ Finalize: Once all settings are configured, click OK to confirm and proceed to the next step.

Water Sanitation is assessed based on the presence of water related features within a raster cell, applying a default 3000m buffer. The scoring is as follows:

Factor Score 0 Score 1 Score 2 Score 3 Score 4 Score 5 Water Sanitation outside the 3km buffer N/A N/A N/A N/A intersection with the 3km buffer

Once every factor has its data, double-click the Place Characterization dimension and follow the same generic pattern as every other item in the tree: assign weights, balance them, and run it.

The outputs (all seven factors and their subfactors, plus their aggregation into the final Place Characterization score) land in the Place Characterization folder within your project folder, on the usual 0–5 enablement scale.

Recap

  • Place Characterization has seven factors; most take point, line or polygon OSM-style data, but Education and Digital Inclusion are driven by a national index score combined with a spatial mask or coverage layer, closer in spirit to the Contextual factors.
  • Several factors (Safety Perception, Active Transport, Water sanitation) offer more than one input option. Pick whichever matches the data you actually have.
  • Results combine into a single Place Characterization output on the usual 0–5 enablement scale.

docs.title: Processor Types
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to recognise which of GeoE3's computation techniques any given indicator uses, and why that determines what kind of data it needs from you.

Every indicator needs to go from whatever raw data it starts with to a 0–5 enablement score for every cell in the grid (see The Model for why that common scale matters). How it gets there depends on which technique the indicator uses. These are the same techniques the PDF analysis report explains in its own Methodology section.

docs.title: National Index Score
docs.text:
Some of what this analysis measures doesn't change from one part of the country to another. Whether the law formally protects women from workplace discrimination, for instance, is set in national legislation: it's true (or not) everywhere at once, down to the last village. For indicators like this, every grid cell is given the same score, taken directly from a published index. A couple of the indicators that work this way are narrowed further, scored only where the underlying data actually applies (only where broadband coverage exists, say, or only inside built-up settlements). Everywhere else is left blank, rather than attaching a labour-force statistic to land where nobody lives, or an internet-use figure to a place the coverage data never reached.

Used by: Workplace Discrimination, Regulatory Frameworks, Financial Inclusion, EPLEX Score (Contextual); Digital Inclusion, Education, Safety Perception when given an index score (Place Characterization).

docs.title: Feature Count
docs.text:
For some indicators, what matters is simply how much of something sits inside each cell of the grid (the number of clinics, say, or the total length of footpaths and cycle lanes running through it). This technique overlays the grid on the real-world data and tallies how many points, lines or polygons fall inside each cell. The score isn't a smooth slide from that count: a cell with nothing nearby scores 0, a cell with exactly one feature scores a middle mark, and a cell with two or more already scores the maximum. A single clinic is enough to lift a cell out of the bottom of the scale; a second one maxes it out.

Used by: Active Transport, at regional and local scale (Place Characterization).

docs.title: Straight-Line Distance
docs.text:
Other indicators are less about density and more about proximity. Can a woman reach a water point without travelling far, or has a violent incident happened nearby? This technique draws a fixed-radius circle around every relevant point, measured as the crow flies rather than along any real path, and scores a grid cell by whether it falls inside that circle or outside it. Being inside the circle is good news for a water point or a bank branch, and bad news for a reported violent event. Whether "inside" means a high score or a low one depends on what's being measured, not on the technique itself.

Used by: FCV, Safety Perception when given street-light points, Water Sanitation (Place Characterization).

docs.title: Distance by Road
docs.text:
For indicators about reaching a service, such as a school, a hospital, or a bus stop, a straight-line circle overstates how accessible a place really is: rivers, dead-end streets and missing roads all make a destination further away in practice than it looks on a map. Rather than measuring as the crow flies, this technique traces the actual road network outward from each facility in several steps (for example a 5-, 10- and 15-minute walk) and scores a grid cell by which travel-time ring it falls inside. The resulting shape hugs the street layout rather than forming a tidy circle. A facility beside the only bridge over a river, for example, reaches much further along the road than it does across the water.

Used by: all five Accessibility factors (Women's Travel Patterns, Access to Public Transport, Health Facilities, Education and Training Facilities, Financial Facilities).

docs.title: Map Value Lookup
docs.text:
Some of the data this analysis draws on arrives as a finished map rather than a set of points or lines (a satellite-derived picture of night-time brightness, say, or a hazard model showing flood risk across the whole country). For indicators like these, there's no counting or buffering to do: each grid cell simply reads off the value already present at that location, the same way you'd read a figure off a weather map by pointing at a city. A brightly lit area scores well on the night-time-lights indicator (used here as a rough proxy for how safe a place feels after dark); a high-risk zone scores poorly on a hazard indicator.

Used by: Environmental Hazards (fire, flood, landslide, cyclone, drought) and Safety Perception when given VIIRS nighttime-lights data.

docs.title: Zone Lookup
docs.text:
A small number of indicators come from boundary data rather than points, lines or a continuous map (a layer of named zones, each carrying its own attribute, such as a safety rating reported by residents). This technique works out which zone a grid cell falls inside, looks up that zone's attribute value in a conversion table, and assigns the matching 0–5 score to every cell inside it. Two cells a street apart can end up with very different scores if they happen to sit on opposite sides of a zone boundary: the result is only ever as fine-grained as the zones it was collected in.

Used by: Digital Inclusion, Education and Safety Perception, when given a classified polygon layer instead of an index score or point data (Place Characterization).

docs.title: Population Share
docs.text:
Occasionally the figure an indicator needs has already been calculated by somebody else and handed over pre-matched to this analysis's own grid (the share of a cell's population living in an urban versus a rural settlement, say, taken from aggregated census-style data). There's no spatial join or buffering left to do: the value is simply attached to the matching grid cell by a shared location key, then rescaled onto the 0–5 scale.

Used by: Education, when backed by Space2Stats' urban/rural split (Place Characterization).

docs.title: Weighted Infrastructure Score
docs.text:
National-scale Active Transport scores a cell differently from every other indicator on this page: rather than taking the single best road or cycle path running through it, every road and cycle path intersecting the cell contributes its own score, weighted by that same score (a well-rated cycle lane counts several times more than a poorly-rated track). A cell crossed by one excellent route and nothing else no longer scores as if it were uniformly excellent, but a cell genuinely dominated by good infrastructure still scores close to the top; a cell with only poor infrastructure stays low even if a single short, better-rated segment clips its edge. Regional and local scale still use the single-best-feature technique described above (Feature Count).

Used by: Active Transport, at national scale only (Place Characterization).

docs.title: Several factors offer more than one technique
docs.text:
Which technique an indicator actually uses often depends on what data you give it. Safety Perception, for instance, can be driven by an index score, street-light points, VIIRS nighttime-lights, or a classified polygon layer, each scored by a different technique above. The dimension walkthroughs that follow spell out exactly which inputs each factor accepts.

Recap

  • Every indicator uses one of these techniques to turn raw data into a 0–5 score: a single published number, counting nearby features, distance to the nearest one, travel time along the road network, a ready-made raster value, a zone lookup, a pre-matched demographic figure, or (Active Transport only, at national scale) a weighted average across every intersecting feature.
  • Several factors support more than one technique; pick whichever matches the data you have.
  • The PDF analysis report's own Methodology section explains whichever of these techniques your analysis actually used.

docs.title: The Analysis Report
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll know how to navigate every section of the PDF analysis report GeoE3 generates after every run, what each page is actually telling you, and how to read the correlation and subnational score matrix pages.

Alongside producing all the different outputs, we also get a PDF report that gets produced. You can pull that up at any time by right-clicking the analysis node and saying Show Analysis Report — it will take a few minutes to generate. This report is a summary of the entire analysis: it tries to cover the high-level results, then describe the methodology, and then provide some more detailed analysis results. The examples on this page are real pages from a Regional-scale Women's Enabling Environments analysis of Portugal.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
It starts off with the credits and attribution: the partners that funded the plugin, and the data attribution for the different data sources we used (OpenStreetMap, OpenRouteService, GHSL, Ookla, Space2Stats, ACLED, VIIRS Nighttime Lights, and whatever you supplied yourself).

Funding partners, who built it, and exactly which data sources contributed to this run.

docs.title: Reading the Maps
docs.text:
Then we describe the legend (the five classes that are key to understanding the different visualizations we produce), using the same 0–5 scale covered in The Model. It also explains what a blank cell means (outside the study area, or no data) versus an actual score of 0: the measured service is genuinely out of reach, e.g. a cell with no road network access.

Very Low Enablement through Highly Enabling, with a one-line description of what each class means in practice.

docs.title: Reading the By-Population Maps
docs.text:
We also have a legend that's used for describing places where results are combined with population — high-density population with low enablement through to high enablement with low density of population — the same 15-class bivariate legend covered on Viewing Your Results.

The colour ramp runs from deep red (low enablement, low population) to light blue (high enablement, high population).

docs.title: Analysis Overview
docs.text:
Then it goes through and shows each of the outputs that got generated. You can see the proportion of cells in the analysis which conform to each of the different enablement classes. In this Portugal run, most of the country sits in moderate enablement, with some areas high and some low.

Overall GeoE3 score across mainland Portugal, Madeira and the Azores, plus the three dimension aggregates underneath.

docs.title: Every Dimension and Factor
docs.text:
We walk through each of the different dimensions in detail. The Contextual dimension factors all come out the same colour across the whole map, because these are flood-filling the whole country with the same value, based on whatever legal framework is in place.

The Contextual Dimension page: Workplace Discrimination, Regulatory Frameworks and Financial Inclusion, each a single flat national score. Accessibility and Place Characterization follow the same per-dimension, then per-factor, pattern, each with its own page.

You can see the breakdown per dimension: very few places score low enablement from high crime or high natural-disaster levels, but there are quite a lot of places with poor accessibility (the red parts toward the sides of the country).

If you configured an aggregation boundary (see Configuring Items), you then get subnational breakdown maps too: the GeoE3 score by administrative region, the same masked by GHSL settlements, and both of those again combined with population. These are the same products available from Add GeoE3 Aggregates to Map on Viewing Your Results.

docs.title: The Subnational Score Matrix
docs.text:
One other thing worth knowing: if you go into Settings → Options → GeoE3, there's a box you can tick, Subnational score matrix. It's an advanced option and it's not on by default — turning it on gets you an additional table in the report, every region and its scoring against every factor, that gives you a way to visualize the economic environment across all the different subnational boundaries and quickly pick out interesting factors.

The table identifies factors by number rather than name, so keep this key page handy, or an aggregation boundary table that maps your region codes to their friendly names.

In this Portugal example run, one factor was red for every single region — that turned out to be a Contextual factor (Regulatory Frameworks, column 4) set to a low value for the whole country. Column 15 (FCV) sits blank throughout: no ACLED or proxy data was supplied for this run, so that factor was excluded rather than scored.

docs.title: Factor Score Patterns
docs.text:
Then you get all of the scores as sparklines, or as charts, in one page that you can view together and pick out any ones where there's particularly high values on one side or the other.

There's probably fairly good transport networks in Portugal, good access to health facilities, training is maybe not so good, and access to financial has got some good areas and some bad areas. Factors driven by a flat national score show a single 100% bar, since a national score has no spatial variation to spread across classes.

docs.title: Low Scores
docs.text:
Then there are some insights: which thing has the biggest ability to improve your access to economic environment? In this Portugal run, Accessibility was the highest one there, the dimension most often limiting a low-scoring cell.

In cells scoring 2 or below, Accessibility was the limiting dimension 100% of the time: distance to services, not legislation or place characteristics, is the single biggest lever for raising those cells a class.

And then there's a part of the analysis that lets you see what the average scores are across the whole study area versus just the areas that are populated.

GHSL settlements cover 35% of the scored study area here and average a noticeably higher score (2.77) than the study area as a whole (2.19). Enablement is concentrated where people actually live.

docs.title: Factor Correlations
docs.text:
There's also an interesting visualization here showing the correlation between factors. If we look at the axis on 13 to 5, there's a negative correlation: environmental hazards and access to public transport negatively impact each other. If we look at the positive side, for example 4 to 10, women's travel patterns and safety perception positively impact each other, so women can travel more comfortably if they've got good safety perception.

Deep navy means the two factors tend to score high in the same places; deep red means one tends to score high where the other scores low; pale or white means no real relationship. The diagonal is always deepest navy (a factor always correlates perfectly with itself) and isn't a finding.

A strong correlation suggests a shared root cause: a single intervention may move both factors at once.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: Then we have a diagram explaining the methodology: taking indicators, weighting them together to form factors, then weighting those factors into dimensions, then weighting the dimensions into the final GeoE3 score (the same cascade covered in The Model). All of the analysis methodology processes are explained in the report too: the Contextual dimension where we fill every cell with the same value, counting features in a cell, buffer analysis, the network analysis that works out a facility's catchment area along the road network, and reading a value straight off an existing map. See Processor Types for the full set, and which indicators in your own analysis used each one.

docs.title: Scoring Weights
docs.text:
All the weights used in the analysis are listed here. Starting from the bottom of a dimension's list: in this Portugal run, Active Transport is assigned 17% of the analysis within Place Characterization, alongside five other factors at 17% each; together they all contribute 45% toward the total global result.

Notice EPLEX and FCV both sit at 0% here: excluded factors still get listed, at zero weight, rather than disappearing from the report.

docs.title: Processing Times
docs.text:
Then the last page has some processing time information. This is useful if you want to go and optimize things, or understand why something isn't running as quickly as you'd like.

Network-isochrone indicators dominate the clock. "Location of hospitals and clinics" alone took almost 4 hours in this regional-scale Portugal run, versus under a minute for most national-score and raster-lookup indicators. Indicators with no data supplied are listed as "not run" rather than omitted.

There are also some notes about the scale and number of grid cells and the region used for the analysis.

Country, scale, number of grid cells, cell size, total area, and the coordinate reference system used.

That's the basics of it, and the real thing you're ultimately getting at the end of the process is the GeoE3 score map, which shows the economic enablement of each cell.

Recap

  • Show Analysis Report on the analysis node generates a full PDF: credits and legends, every output with its distribution, subnational breakdowns, a factor correlation heatmap, and the methodology and weights actually used.
  • The correlation heatmap: navy means two factors move together, red means they move in opposite directions, pale means no real relationship.
  • The Subnational score matrix setting (Settings → Options → GeoE3, off by default) adds a key page plus a region-by-factor colour grid. A column that's one solid colour everywhere is almost always a flat national (Contextual) score, not a mistake.
  • Factor Score Patterns, Low Scores, and Settlement and Hazard Patterns surface things the blended dimension and GeoE3 scores can smooth over, worth a look even when the headline map looks fine.

Next: Sharing Your Results, getting the raw grid out of QGIS and into a spreadsheet, CSV or other GIS software.

docs.title: Running the Analysis
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to kick off a full analysis run, choose between Run All and Run Incomplete, and know what happens (and how to recover) if a long run gets interrupted.

Once every dimension is configured (see the three previous pages), you're ready to run the whole analysis.

docs.title: Run All vs Run Incomplete
docs.text:
Start the whole thing running from the Run All button at the bottom of the panel, or Run Incomplete to skip anything that's already finished. Run All gives a warning that any previous analysis you've done will be deleted; it will not delete the working files you've made, but it will delete any analysis outputs. It then works through every indicator, factor and dimension in order, calculating scores across the grid, and loads each result onto the map as it completes.

To rerun a single item after changing something, right-click it and choose Clear Item, then right-click again and, holding Shift, choose Run Item Workflow. This is covered already on The Interface.

docs.title: This can take a while
docs.text: Depending on the size of the country and whether you're running a regional, national or local-scale analysis, a full run can take a while, particularly for a large country at national or local grid resolution. Leave it running in the background rather than expecting it to finish in a few seconds.

docs.title: If something interrupts it
docs.text:
The project saves its progress to disk as each item finishes, not just at the end of the whole run, so a crash doesn't throw away work that's already done. If QGIS crashes, or you need to shut down or restart the computer partway through a run, reopen the project afterwards and click Run Incomplete rather than Run All: it picks up from whichever indicator, factor or dimension it reached, instead of starting the whole analysis over from scratch.

Recap

  • Run All runs everything and clears previous outputs first; Run Incomplete only runs what hasn't finished yet.
  • A full run can take a while on a large country or a fine grid. Let it run in the background.
  • Progress is saved to disk after every item completes. If QGIS crashes or the computer restarts mid-run, reopen the project and click Run Incomplete to carry on rather than starting over.

docs.title: Sharing Your Results
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll be able to get GeoE3's raw grid results out of QGIS (as a vector or raster layer, or exported to CSV), and know where every file an analysis produced actually lives on disk.

One last thing worth showing is how to access the raw data that's produced. GeoE3 adds layer groups to your project with a nested structure similar to the model tree. You can see all the outputs for each dimension, and each one shows the details relating to it. Right-click over any node and you'll see a whole bunch of menu items starting with Add (the same right-click menu introduced on The Interface):

  • Add GeoE3 Score to Map: either a vector grid or a raster grid. If you want to work with the vector grid, you can go and look in its attribute table and see all of the indices that were calculated across the whole study area. Export this to a CSV, take it to your AI application or a spreadsheet, and do further numerical interpretation using that software.
  • Add GeoE3 Aggregates to Map: the subnational breakdown, like you saw in the PDF report. If you use the Identify tool you can click on any one of these and see the area name and the majority score, basically the highest score for the region.
  • There are more products in the menu too: outputs masked by job opportunities, the global human settlements layer used for the settlements masking, and so on.
  • Open Working Directory takes you to the place where all of the analytical outputs were produced, including the reports and all of the data sets that were made during the analysis.

docs.title: The study area grid
docs.text:
The foundation underneath every one of these outputs is the study_area/ GeoPackage created back when you created the project: the regular grid (hexagons for a regional analysis, square cells for national or local) that every indicator, factor, dimension and the final GeoE3 Score is calculated against. You can hand that GeoPackage to a colleague who wants to build their own analysis on the same spatial framework.

Recap

  • The raw grid is yours to use beyond QGIS. Add it as a vector layer and export its attribute table to CSV for further analysis elsewhere.
  • Add GeoE3 Aggregates to Map gets you the subnational breakdown; the Identify tool reads off each region's name and majority score.
  • Open Working Directory gets you straight to every file this analysis produced, including the study_area/ GeoPackage every output is built on.

That should get you up and running with the basics of using the GeoE3 plugin, from an empty QGIS install through to a finished, reportable analysis. There are more things you can do beyond this walkthrough: the Legacy Detailed Reference covers a few individual factors in more granular detail, and About has the background on the framework this tool implements.

If you'd like to get in touch (feedback, questions, or to help), the Acknowledgements page has contact details for the team.

docs.title: The Model
docs.text:
Learning objective

By the end of this page you'll understand the four levels of the GeoE3 model (indicator, factor, dimension and analysis), how weights aggregate one level into the next, and why every score, at every level, lands on the same 0–5 Likert scale.

docs.title: Indicators, factors, dimensions and analysis
docs.text:
The model tree you met on The Interface page organises every output into three categories, which we call dimensions: the Contextual dimension, the Accessibility dimension and the Place Characterization dimension. Those are further subdivided into factors (the second-level grouping), and each dimension may have one or more factors associated with it.

  • Dimensions: there are 3 (Contextual, Accessibility, Place Characterization), the broadest grouping, each with its own weight in the final score.
  • Factors: there are 16 across the three dimensions, the themes you'll configure one by one (e.g. Workplace Discrimination, Women's Travel Patterns, Active Transport).
  • Indicators: there are 35 in total, the actual calculated layers. Most factors are a single indicator. A couple of them (Women's Travel Patterns and Environmental Hazards) expand into five indicators each: childcare, schools, groceries, pharmacies and green space for the former; fire, flood, landslide, cyclone and drought for the latter.

Every grid cell in an analysis has a score from 0 to 5 for each indicator, combined into factor, dimension and overall scores. This is the same diagram the PDF report opens its Methodology section with:

Indicators → Factor → Dimension → GeoE3 Score, each step combined by a weight you assign. The population and opportunities-mask filters on the right are covered in Configuring Items.

Every level of that cascade works the same way: you assign a weight to each child item, and the tool combines them into its parent's score.

  • Indicators → Factor: a factor's indicators are combined using the weights you assign them (most factors have only one indicator, so this step is invisible; Women's Travel Patterns and Environmental Hazards are the exceptions, each combining five).
  • Factors → Dimension: each dimension's factors are weighted and combined the same way. Double-click a dimension to see and change those weights.
  • Dimensions → Analysis: the three dimensions are weighted and combined into the final GeoE3 Score, the same pattern one level up again.

Whenever you change a weight, the total of the weight values must add up to one. If it doesn't, the weight values are shown in red and you can't confirm the dialog. If you want to assign every enabled item an equal weight, press Balance Weights rather than typing each value by hand. This applies the same way whether you're balancing indicators within a factor, factors within a dimension, or dimensions within the analysis. The mechanics of opening an item's dialog, setting weights, excluding items you don't have data for, and running the workflow are covered once, generically, in Configuring Items, since they're the same regardless of which level of the tree you're working on.

docs.title: The 0–5 Likert scale
docs.text:
Every indicator, factor, dimension and the final analysis score all land on the same scale: each cell gets a score of enabling or not enabling, on a scale of 0 to 5 (blue is enabling, red is not enabling). This is the same 5-class legend used to colour every result layer in the plugin:

Score Class Colour 0 – 1 Very Low Enablement 1 – 2 Low Enablement 2 – 3 Moderately Enabling 3 – 4 Enabling 4 – 5 Highly Enabling

When you run the final analysis, the result comes through in this same Likert scale: red cells are very low economic enablement, orange is low, yellow is intermediate, green is enabling, and blue is very enabling.

The completed model tree, with the final GeoE3 Score on the same 0–5 scale as everything beneath it.

Rescaling every indicator onto the same 0–5 range (whether the underlying data was a percentage, a distance in metres, a travel time, or a published index score out of 100) is what makes it valid to combine completely different kinds of data into one number. How each indicator actually gets converted onto that scale depends on what kind of data it starts from. That's the subject of the next page, Processor Types.

Recap

  • Four levels: indicator → factor → dimension → analysis. Each level combines its children using weights you assign, the same way every time.
  • At any level, the weights must add up to one (shown in red if they don't). Balance Weights resets every enabled item to an equal share rather than normalising whatever you'd typed in.
  • Every score, at every level, lands on the same 0–5 enablement scale: 0–1 Very Low Enablement through to 4–5 Highly Enabling.
